Future work should aim to enhance perioperative safety, monitoring, and documentation in regional anesthesia by adopting standardized tools and reporting frameworks. One priority area is the broader implementation of objective injection pressure monitoring devices such as the BSmart™ Injection Pressure Monitor (B. Braun Medical, Melsungen, Germany) and the SAFIRA ® —SAFer Injection for Regional Anaesthesia system (Medovate Ltd., Cambridge, UK) [ , , ]. The BSmart™ device provides inline, colour-coded feedback on injection pressure during peripheral nerve blocks, offering an objective and quantifiable alternative to subjective “syringe feel” and facilitating documentation of injection pressures within predefined ranges. Similarly, the SAFIRA ® system integrates a safety mechanism that automatically limits the maximum injection pressure and allows the clinician to control both aspiration and infusion with a single operator workflow, potentially reducing the risk of injection at pressures associated with neural injury. Regular audits and feedback cycles, along with periodic reviews of checklist items and outcome data, will help monitor compliance and identify areas for improvement. Finally, involving frontline clinicians in ongoing updates will strengthen ownership, reduce resistance, and foster a sustainable safety culture within regional anesthesia practice. An additional important determinant of real-world effectiveness is checklist adherence. The potential clinical and organizational benefits described in the theoretical model assume appropriate and consistent implementation. Variability in compliance rates across institutions may significantly influence outcomes, as demonstrated in other checklist based safety interventions. Future prospective studies should therefore assess not only complication trends but also checklist utilization rates and quality of completion, in order to better understand the relationship between adherence and safety impact. 4.2. Strengths and Limitations The questionnaire consisted of structured multiple-choice items using Likert-scale response options (ranging from strong disagreement to strong agreement). Questions addressed perceived necessity of a regional anesthesia checklist, expected impact on patient safety, educational value, and potential medico-legal benefits. The survey was exploratory and descriptive in nature and was not designed as a validated psychometric instrument. (We added survey results in ) This study adds to the expanding field of safety standardization in regional anesthesia by introducing a carefully developed checklist and a new method for evaluating its impact in healthcare institutions. One of the study’s key strengths is its dual focus: the LRA checklist was created and validated through expert consensus, while also being situated within a broader framework that considers workflow efficiency, legal protection, and organizational value. By incorporating a theoretical model, the study provides a fresh perspective for decision-makers, which could enhance administrative acceptance, an aspect that is often overlooked in literature on checklists. Model parameters were based on conservative, literature-informed assumptions and institutional plausibility ranges rather than empirical prospective data. The estimated absolute reduction in complication probability (ΔPerror) was modeled using cautious ranges extrapolated from published evidence on checklist-based safety interventions in perioperative settings. The documentation-related benefit (Cdoc) was conceptualized as a proxy for improved medico-legal traceability and risk mitigation, acknowledging that such benefits are difficult to quantify directly. These parameters were intentionally conservative to avoid overestimation of economic impact. The model is therefore intended as a structured decision-support framework rather than a formal cost-effectiveness analysis. A one-way sensitivity analysis was performed to explore the robustness of the model under conservative and plausible variations in key assumptions. In addition to varying the relative reduction in complication-related costs (20–40%), we varied net time saved per procedure (1–3 min) and examined the effect of different annual procedure volumes in scaling scenarios. All other parameters were held constant. This approach allowed assessment of model stability without introducing excessive analytical complexity. However, the study does have limitations. It does not include real-world implementation data, so the projected benefits remain theoretical. The model also fails to account for cultural, behavioral, or organizational factors that can significantly influence the adoption of safety tools. Furthermore, the checklist was specifically tailored to the Italian healthcare setting, which may limit its generalizability until it is adapted and tested in other healthcare systems. Future research should focus on multicenter validation, assessing user compliance over time, and evaluating the checklist’s impact on clinical outcomes, team performance, and training effectiveness. 5. Its creation followed a rigorous methodology, which included expert validation of the content. Additionally, a theoretical model suggested potential organizational and economic benefits for healthcare institutions. While these findings are preliminary, they support the integration of the LRA checklist into routine clinical practice as part of a larger patient safety strategy. The effectiveness of checklist implementation should be evaluated through prospective audits measuring adherence to checklist items, quality of documentation, and trends in complication recognition. Future steps include multicenter implementation studies and quality-improvement initiatives comparing safety indicators before and after checklist adoption, in order to quantify its real-world clinical impact. chunks.content: Introduction The basic principle of inferior vena cava filter (IVCF) is to intercept the shedding of venous thrombus through the umbrella, spindle or spiral shaped filter structure, so as to prevent lethal acute pulmonary embolism (PE) [ , ]. At present, retrievable filters are the mainstream of clinical application. However, complications following filter placement, including inferior vena cava filter thrombosis (IVCFT), filter displacement or fracture, and perforation or occlusion of the inferior vena cava, often lead to significant morbidity and mortality. Of them, IVCFT is one of common complications and it can be as high as 31% [ , ]. While timely retrieval of IVCF could reduce the incidence of complications [ , ], retrieval of the filter is often delayed in clinical practice in that most of the patients are asymptomatic even after forming IVCF thrombosis. IVCFT may lead to filter indwelling or retrieval failure, and anti-coagulation is insufficient for the IVCFT treatment. Therefore, mechanical retrieval of the IVCF thrombosis as well as the filters has been developed and applied in the clinical practice. In this regard, manual aspiration thrombectomy (MAT), catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT), AngioJet rheolytic thrombectomy (ART), balloon dilatation and stent implantation are the most used endovascular intervention therapies for IVCFT [ – ]. While various endovascular techniques such as MAT, CDT, ART, and stent placement have been previously reported for the management of IVCFT [ – ], the existing literature primarily focuses on the outcomes of these techniques applied in isolation. A significant knowledge gap exists regarding the efficacy, safety, and logistical outcomes of employing a tailored, multi-modal approach, where these techniques are selectively combined based on specific thrombus characteristics. In addition, the application of such an algorithmic strategy and its subsequent mid-term results are poorly documented in detailed, single-center experiences. The current study was therefore designed to address this gap by retrospectively analyzing the feasibility and safety of a comprehensive, patient-specific endovascular strategy for IVCFT. To accomplish this, we have developed a series of step-by-step and individualized treatment strategies for IVCFT. Here, we report the outcomes of 31 patients with IVCFT treated with either a single modality or a combination of MAT, CDT, ART, and stenting. Materials and methods Patients This was a retrospective study performed in the Suzhou Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). Patients with IVCFT, who were treated and followed up in the hospital from January 2020 to December 2022, were enrolled and analyzed in this study. All patients had indications and met criteria for inferior vena cava filter placement, which were published in the Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Deep Venous Thrombosis (2017 version) [ ]. The indications included: (1) imaging confirmed the presence of floating thrombus in iliac, femoral or inferior vena cava ( n = 31); (2) For acute DVT, catheter contact thrombolysis (CDT) or mechanical thrombectomy (PMT) was proposed as the initial treatment ( n = 5); (3) High risk patients who have been diagnosed with acute DVT and complicated with major trauma/fracture and need to undergo lower limb or pelvic orthopedic surgery within a time limit ( n = 26). All patients received anti-coagulation treatment after the filter implantation. Prior to the endovascular therapeutic procedure, patients and their families were informed the potential outcomes and risks of each procedure, and a written consent was obtained from the patients or legal guidance. Patients’ demographic information including age, BMI, and gender as well as risk factors for deep venous thrombosis (DVT), affected limbs, underlying disease, family history, and clinical symptoms were collected. In addition, the type of IVCF used and maximum diameter of the thrombi were also collected. This study was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Suzhou TCM Hospital. Pre-procedural assessment and anti-coagulation regimen Anticoagulant therapy with low molecular weight heparin (100 U/kg, subcutaneous injection, q12h) was given during the perioperative period. Rivaroxaban (15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks, followed by 20 mg once daily) was administered orally for at least 3 months after discharge. If the thrombus exceeded the tip of the IVCF, a second retrievable IVCF was placed above the primary filter via the jugular vein or femoral vein to prevent fatal PE caused by the thrombus detachment from the top of primary filter. After the procedure, the primary IVCF was retrieved if there was no obvious filling defect or the maximum diameter of thrombus was smaller than 6 mm [ ]. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) As a basic thrombolytic method, CDT is suitable for acute or sub-acute thrombosis. In this study, if the thrombus was widely loaded, or the limited effect of MAT alone was anticipated, CDT was preferably applied. For some residual thrombus after primary treatment by MAT or ART, CDT was also used to further dissolve the thrombus. CDT was performed using the Fountain thrombolytic catheter (Merit Medical Systems, Inc, USA). Briefly, a catheter was delivered to the site of filter thrombus via the femoral vein on the side of affected limb. The catheter was left in place and urokinase (400,000~600,000 U per 24 hours) was infused with micropump continuously. Inferior vena cava angiography was performed every 48 to 72 hours to reassess the size and location of the filter thrombus. Further treatment was conducted if the thrombolytic outcome was not met the following endpoints of thrombolysis: (1) The thrombus disappeared, or maximum diameter of the thrombus was < 6 mm. (2) Two consecutive angiograms showed no change in the thrombus. In addition, further treatment was conducted if the patient experienced serious complications such as massive bleeding during the treatment. ART is used to quickly and effectively reduce the thrombus load, the risk of pulmonary embolism, and the dose of thrombolytic medication. In this study, ART was usually combined with CDT. It was applied after establishing the channel via the anterior tibial vein or femoral vein. The power-pulsed spraying thrombolytic mode was used, and 200,000 U urokinase was injected into the inferior vena cava thrombus or intra-filter thrombosis at a speed of 1 mm/s. After 20 min, a mechanical rheolytic thrombectomy was then performed to remove the thrombus by aspiration. This procedure was repeated 2 to 3 times. CDT was further performed if a residual thrombosis was found after the ART procedure. The procedure and a representative outcome of ART was illustrated in Fig. . The 31 patients with IVCFT were enrolled into this study. As shown in Table , majority of the IVCFT located at femoral vein (18 cases) followed by iliac vein (12 cases) and inferior vena cava (1 case). Most of the 31 patients had morbidities, that is, 28 had bone fracture, 23 had hypertension, 17 had diabetes, and 15 had dyslipidemia. However, only 7 of them had clinical symptoms associated with venous thrombosis, that is, swelling and pain in the legs (4 cases) or shoulder and back pain (3 cases). Alteration of hemodynamics due to IVCF implantation; 3). Vascular tissue recognizes IVCF as a foreign body; 4). The dislodged thrombus from distance vein was caught by the filter; 5). Size of the thrombi was 11–30 mm in maximum diameter, and majority of them located either inside the filters or underneath the filters, indicating majority of the thrombi could be the dislodged and caught by the filters when they flew into the inferior vena cava from a distance vein. Most of the patients with IVCFT are asymptomatic, and approximately 30% of the patients have clinical symptoms [ ]. In the circumstances where IVCFT is suspected, venography by computed tomography (CT) is a useful diagnostic approach in defining the extent of clot and choosing a management from various endovascular intervention strategies. In this study, clinical symptoms, including swelling and pain in the legs or shoulder and back pain, were found in 22.5% (7 out of 31 cases), and contrast angiography was performed in all 31 cases to determine the location and extent of the clots. We could not distinguish whether the symptoms of the 7 patients in this study were caused by new IVCF or they were the sequelae of previous VTE. However, in the current study, the intervention was decided mainly based on the fact whether the symptoms were new or acute exacerbation following filter implantation, or whether they were associated with IVCFT due to significant blockade of blood flow confirmed by imaging. This clinical judgment constituted the basis of intervention therapy to thrombus removal and restore venous patency. MAT can not only quickly remove a thrombus from IVCF and minimize the risk of thrombus shedding in the process of filter retrieval but also reduce bleeding and other complications caused by thrombolysis. For IVCF with small thrombus and poor thrombolytic response, MAT has better feasibility and safety. Furthermore, given that an IVCF engaged with a small thrombus (defined as a thrombus with a maximum diameter of less than 10 mm) can often be removed en bloc , application of MAT prior to filter retrieval can significantly improve the safety and feasibility of the procedure by minimizing the thrombus burden [ , ]. However, the followings should be kept in mind in the application of manual aspiration: location of the thrombus should be identified prior to the procedure; direction and position of the sheath head should be instantly adjustable during the procedure; bleeding must be controlled effectively during and post-procedure. In addition, avoiding aspiration of the inferior vena cava wall by mistake is crucial. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) enables a localized delivery of thrombolytic agents directly into the thrombus, which dramatically improves the thrombolytic efficiency, prevents post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), facilitates restoration of venous patency without increasing risk of heavy hemorrhage, and reduces the risk of recurrence [ , ]. CDT is often applied for the IVCFT patients with acute or subacute thrombus, for which CDT could be a curative therapy [ , ]. The choice of thrombolytic agent and the dose used remains variable although tPA or urokinase are most used. In the current study, favorable outcomes were achieved in the following respective treatment groups: in all 6 cases (6/6) treated with MAT alone, all 10 cases (10/10) treated with CDT alone, and all 7 cases (7/7) treated with the combination of MAT and CDT. Mechanical thrombectomy plus CDT could significantly improve thrombus removal and aid in lysis of residual thrombus [ , ]. AngioJet rheolytic thrombectomy (ART) is one of the commonly used devices to perform mechanical thrombectomy, especially, for the IVCFT patients with a large thrombus burden. ART can quickly and effectively remove thrombus in the filter, reduce thrombus burden, relieve venous obstruction, and protect valve function [ , , ]. Adding ART to CDT can shorten thrombolytic time, reduce urokinase dosage and reduce bleeding risk [ , , ]. However, discomfort such as chest tightness and palpitation may occur during the ART procedure, and transient hemoglobinuria could be seen post-ART procedure, which may result from the damage of red blood cells and intravascular hemolysis. In the current study, 5 cases (16%) were treated with ART plus CDT, and 2 cases (3%) were treated with combination of ART, CDT and MAT. In these 7 cases, post-ART angiography indicated that the clot size was significantly reduced, and the blood flow was remarkably restored compared to that of pre-ART. Findings of the current study indicated that ART followed by CDT treatment could not only prevent the clot in the hidden site but also result in curative outcomes for the patients with IVCFT. Technical success of endovascular intervention and achievement of venous patency for the IVCF thrombosis are largely depending on the time interval from onset to intervention. In this regard, while CDT and MAT are often used for patients at acute or sub-acute phase IVCFT, they are not suitable for the treatment of chronic and organized IVCFT. For the treatment of latter case, balloon dilatation and stent implantation may be the best option [ – ]. In the current study, with the timely diagnosis of IVCFT and considering cost of the procedure, most of the cases were treated with MAT, CDT, and ART alone or in combination 2 or 3 methods, and only one patient was treated with CDT plus balloon dilatation and stent implantation, whose clinical symptoms were not significantly improved after the CDT alone. Nevertheless, after combined treatment with balloon dilatation following CDT and stent implantation, favorable outcome was achieved in this patient, suggesting balloon dilatation and stent implantation plus CDT be effective for the treatment of chronic IVCFT. It has been reported that the residual thrombus of IVCFT may not increase the risk of fatal PE or other serious complications if the thrombus is < 10 mm in diameter [ ]. Considering the anatomy and the inner diameter of the filter sheath as well as referring literature [ , ], the filter with thrombus size smaller than 10 mm in diameter could be directly removed. Therefore, in this study, we set the criteria for residual IVCFT < 10 mm in maximum diameter and no obvious filling defects. Following these criteria, the IVCFT was successfully removed in all 31 cases of this study. Therefore, in this study, we set the criteria for residual IVCFT < 10 mm in maximum diameter and no obvious filling defects. Following these criteria, the IVCFT was successfully removed in all 31 cases of this study. However, thread-like or fragmentary thrombi remained in 12 cases, and majority of them were old thrombi with a small number of fresh thrombi on the surface. Although a secondary retrievable IVCF was used prior to the MAT procedure in a previously reported study [ ], we do not recommend such a conservative treatment because it may increase unnecessary economic burden to the patients. For the patient with a IVCFT caught inside the filter that could be treated with MAT or ART alone, applying a secondary IVCF is less important. However, in the case of a large clot that extends out to the top of the primary IVC filter, placement of a secondary retrievable IVCF prior to the endovascular intervention procedures is necessary to prevent pulmonary embolism by the dislodged thrombus from top of the primary filters. In the current study, a large volume thrombus was found on top of the IVC filter in 6 out 31 cases. A 2 nd retrievable IVC filter was applied prior to the endovascular intervention therapies in all the 6 cases. After clearing the IVCF thrombus, the primary filter was firstly removed, and then the secondary filter was removed 2 to 4 days later to minimize the possibility of PE complication. Favorable therapeutic results were achieved in all 6 cases without visible thrombus caught by the secondary IVCF. Our experience suggested that the trans-jugular approach could avoid thrombus detachment due to manual manipulation. All 31 cases were followed up for up to 6 months post the procedures. Neither recurrent thrombosis, nor symptomatic PE was found during the following up period in any case, suggesting endovascular intervention strategies applied in the current study for the patients with IVCFT were effective and safe. Given that asymptomatic PE occurred in all patients in this study, its prevalence in the IVCFT population may be high. Future prospective studies using systematic screening are needed to clarify the true incidence of asymptomatic PE and its implications for treatment strategies. In addition, side effect of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) may occur in the patients receiving heparin anti-coagulation during the procedures. In the current study, however, none of the 31 cases had developed HIT. There were limitations in this study. First, it was a single-center retrospective study with small sample size, which could be prone to patient selection bias and subjective judgment bias for thrombus removal. Second, patients were not randomly assigned to various treatment strategies, which could be another biased study design. Third, this study provided preliminary outcomes of 6-month follow-up, which was relatively short. Fourth, due to the limited symptomatic cohort (only 7 out of 31 patients presented with clinical symptoms), postoperative clinical symptoms were not systematically assessed. Fifth, while we believe majority of the thrombi in this study were intercepted by IVC filter, because majority of them located above or inside the filters, thrombi formed in situ of the filters were not excluded in this study. Finally, the inferior vena cava diameter was not systematically measured; therefore, the thrombus-to-vein ratio, a hemodynamically relevant measure of thrombus burden, could not be calculated. The IVC diameter can be variable and is influenced by acute thrombosis, making retrospective measurement challenging. Given those limitations, findings of the current study remain to be further confirmed with well-designed prospective studies in the future. Conclusion Taken together, this retrospective study demonstrated that a tailored, multimodal endovascular intervention approach, including strategies such as manual aspiration thrombectomy (MAT), catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT), AngioJet rheolytic thrombectomy (ART), and stent implantation, is a highly effective and safe management for inferior vena cava filter thrombosis (IVCFT). Combination therapies (CDT + MAT or ART + CDT) were particularly effective for managing diverse thrombus burdens and morphologies, suggesting these endovascular interventions could be a standard approach for IVCFT to reduce long-term morbidity associated with filter-related thrombosis.

Introduction Regional anesthesia (RA) has become an essential component of modern perioperative care, offering effective pain relief, decreasing opioid use, and facilitating early recovery [ , ]. The increasing use of ultrasound guidance, continuous techniques, and multimodal perioperative pathways has significantly improved patient outcomes, but it has also added complexity and medico-legal considerations to regional anesthesia procedures [ , ]. In this evolving landscape, incorporating principles of precision medicine and clinical risk management tools has become fundamental to contemporary anesthetic practice. Over the last decade, the introduction of structured checklists has emerged as an important innovation in surgery, reflecting a broader trend towards safety standardization within perioperative medicine [ ]. Checklists serve several purposes: they help prevent avoidable neurological injuries and other complications by ensuring adherence to safety protocols, and they enhance communication among anesthesia and surgical teams [ , , ]. Their medico-legal significance lies not only in error prevention but also in documenting the safety culture and clinical reasoning that support each procedure. Among the potential adverse events associated with regional anesthesia, neurological injury is considered the most serious and feared complication. Although these injuries are rare, with an estimated incidence of 0.02% to 0.4% depending on the type of block and the patient population, they can lead to prolonged disabilities and legal consequences [ ]. The pathophysiology of neurological injuries is often multifactorial, involving mechanical trauma, ischemic injury, or neurotoxicity from local anesthetics. These complications may be exacerbated by inadequate monitoring or insufficient procedural vigilance. Appropriate monitoring, including standard hemodynamic monitoring, ultrasound guidance during block performance, and structured post-procedural observation, can support early detection of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), vascular puncture, or neurological complications, thereby reducing their severity and clinical impact. Structured checklists can play a vital role in this regard by ensuring systematic pre-procedural verification, appropriate technique selection, continuous patient monitoring, and thorough post-block evaluation [ ]. In the Italian healthcare context, variability in documentation practices, organizational models, and medico-legal expectations may further increase the need for structured safety tools. A standardized checklist can improve safety by ensuring consistent adherence to key procedural steps, promoting team communication, strengthening traceability, and supporting risk management. These tools help standardize practices, improve communication among team members, and reduce the likelihood of avoidable neurological damage. Numerous studies have shown that structured checklists can reduce adverse events, such as neurological damage and perioperative morbidity [ ]. Likewise, anesthesia-specific checklists have been proven to reduce human error and improve team communication and compliance with safety standards [ ]. In this context, the LRA checklist was developed and endorsed by the Board of the Italian chapter of the European Society of Regional Anaesthesia and Pain Therapy. This checklist is intended to guide clinicians through all stages of regional anesthesia, from patient identification and obtaining consent to post-procedural assessment. It incorporates principles of precision medicine, interdisciplinary communication, and clinical risk mitigation. This article presents initial data on the implementation of the LRA checklist at a tertiary university hospital. Additionally, it provides a brief review of existing literature concerning the preventive and legal benefits of utilizing checklist-based safety systems in regional anesthesia. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Phase 1—Preliminary Survey An initial exploratory survey was distributed to all members of the ESRA Italian Chapter in October 2023 during the ESRA Italian Chapter Meeting in Palermo. The purpose of the questionnaire was to evaluate the perceived need for, and potential usefulness of, a standardized checklist for regional anesthesia procedures within the Italian clinical context. Respondents were asked whether they believed that a checklist was important for enhancing safety, documentation, and training during the execution of both peripheral and central nerve blocks. 2.2. Phase 2—Working Group Formation and Review of International Models To ensure content validity and expert consensus on the checklist items, a modified Delphi process was conducted. Fifteen members of the ESRA Italian Chapter Board (2024) with recognized expertise in regional anesthesia independently evaluated each checklist item using a 5-point Likert scale (from 1 = “not relevant” to 5 = “highly relevant”). Agreement of ≥75% on scores ≥4 was predefined as the threshold for consensus. After the first round, aggregated anonymized feedback was shared with the panel, and a second evaluation round was performed to refine items and enhance clarity and clinical applicability. The process resulted in minor modifications and confirmed the clinical relevance, clarity, and feasibility of all checklist domains. This validation approach ensured the checklist’s methodological rigor and supported its adoption for pilot testing in Italian university hospitals. The LRA checklist was developed in accordance with internationally recognized frameworks for checklist creation in healthcare [ , , , ]. The process was structured into six key steps as reported in . Phase 3—Adaptation to the Italian Context The structure and content of the ASRA checklist were carefully analyzed to ensure alignment with Italian regulatory standards, clinical practices, and medico-legal requirements. Modifications were made to incorporate national terminology, procedural workflows, and institutional safety protocols commonly used in Italian hospitals. The resulting draft checklist was designed to address all procedural phases, from patient identification and informed consent to post-procedural monitoring, while remaining concise and user-friendly. 2.4. Phase 4—Validation by ESRA Italian Chapter Board The adapted version of the LRA checklist was then submitted for critical evaluation and approval by the ESRA Italian Chapter Board. Board members reviewed the document for clinical completeness, clarity, and feasibility of implementation. Minor revisions were made based on the Board’s feedback, resulting in a final version approved for dissemination and pilot testing in selected university hospitals as reported in . 2.5. Preliminary Survey and ESRA Italian Chapter Board Evaluation Before the Board evaluation, the perceived need for a standardized regional anesthesia checklist was assessed through an exploratory survey distributed to all ESRA Italian Chapter members. The panel members were selected among the ESRA Italian Chapter Board based on predefined criteria, including recognized clinical expertise in regional anesthesia, active practice in high-volume centers, involvement in education and guideline development, and representation of both academic and non-academic institutions across different geographic regions of Italy. All experts had more than 10 years of clinical experience in regional anesthesia. The composition of the panel aimed to ensure diversity of institutional settings while maintaining high-level technical competence, thereby minimizing potential selection bias and enhancing content validity. After the first round of reviews, we analyzed the aggregated anonymized feedback and made minor adjustments to enhance clarity and usability. These changes included refining the wording to eliminate ambiguity, clearly specifying the selected documentation fields, and ensuring consistency in terminology across all sections of the checklist. The questionnaire aimed to evaluate clinicians’ opinions on the utility, feasibility, and perceived impact of implementing a structured checklist in daily practice. 3. Results A total of 144 respondents participated, representing 102 different institutions. The majority expressed a high level of agreement regarding the importance of introducing a structured tool to enhance safety, documentation accuracy, and teaching consistency. The evaluation involved 15 board members from 15 different Italian hospitals and universities. Specifically, 100% of respondents considered the checklist essential for improving patient safety and reducing avoidable errors, while 75% viewed it as a valuable support for training residents in regional anesthesia techniques Several respondents also emphasized its potential medico-legal value, particularly for documenting adherence to institutional safety protocols (see also ). Following this positive feedback, the preliminary version of the “Anestesia Locoregionale (LRA)” Checklist ( ) was developed and submitted to the ESRA Italy Board for critical review. 3.1. Theoretical Impact Model To complement the qualitative assessment, a simplified theoretical model was developed to estimate the potential organizational and economic impact of implementing the LRA checklist in clinical practice The model was conceived as a pragmatic and reproducible framework to explore how checklist adoption might translate into time optimization, complication reduction, and cost containment, without requiring complex statistical inputs. The approach was designed to remain simple and adaptable, allowing institutions to reproduce the analysis using a limited number of variables, including annual procedure volume (N), staff cost per minute, estimated time savings, baseline complication rate, expected relative risk reduction, and average complication management cost. The resulting economic effect was computed through the following expression: Net Benefit = N × [(Cerror × ΔPerror) + (Ctime × ΔT) + Cdoc − Crun] − Cimpl where N = number of regional anesthesia procedures performed per year; C error = mean cost per complication; Δ P error = absolute reduction in complication probability; C time = staff cost per minute; Δ T = net procedural time saved (minutes); C doc = average medico-legal benefit from improved documentation; C run = marginal cost per checklist use; C impl = one-off cost for checklist implementation and training. A simple one-way sensitivity analysis was performed to explore the robustness of the theoretical model. Key assumptions were varied within plausible ranges, including the relative reduction in complication-related costs (20–40%), net time saved per procedure

A simple one-way sensitivity analysis was performed to explore the robustness of the theoretical model. Key assumptions were varied within plausible ranges, including the relative reduction in complication-related costs (20–40%), net time saved per procedure (1–3 min), and annual procedural volume in scaling scenarios. Under conservative assumptions, the model remained generally neutral-to-favorable, with estimated annual net benefits ranging approximately from €5000 to €18,000 (for 1000 procedures/year). These calculations should be interpreted as illustrative rather than predictive, as real-world effects will depend on implementation quality, adherence, and local institutional context ( case scenario). For this theoretical model, “preventable complications” are defined as adverse events that could potentially be mitigated through adherence to standardized safety procedures outlined in the checklist. These complications include, but are not limited to: local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), procedures performed on the incorrect site or for the wrong indication, dosage miscalculations, failure to recognize early neurological symptoms, and documentation errors that affect medico-legal accountability. “Workflow optimization” refers to potential improvements in procedural efficiency that stem from a structured sequence of safety checks, standardized communication, and the elimination of redundant documentation steps. These concepts serve as parameters for theoretical modeling and were not directly measured as clinical endpoints in this study. 3.2. A Case Scenario A baseline scenario was simulated using conservative and realistic assumptions for a tertiary university hospital: The model suggests that checklist implementation may generate incremental efficiency gains and risk reduction benefits. However, these estimates are illustrative rather than predictive. The primary value of the model lies in providing a structured framework for institutional evaluation rather than precise economic forecasting. These findings indicate that even modest improvements in procedural safety and the standardization of workflows can provide significant economic and organizational benefits for healthcare institutions. 3.3. Interpretation The model demonstrates that the implementation of the LRA checklist can be economically advantageous, primarily through improved efficiency and prevention of adverse events. Its simplicity makes it a practical decision-support tool for hospitals seeking to quantify the benefits of structured safety interventions in regional anesthesia. Although theoretical, these results align with published evidence showing that checklist-based safety systems improve perioperative outcomes and reduce overall healthcare costs. Prospective multicenter validation will be necessary to confirm the model’s predictive reliability in real-world settings ( ). 4. Discussion Checklists are widely acknowledged as crucial safety tools in high-risk industries. They promote standardization, reduce human error, and improve team communication. In aviation, for example, checklists are a fundamental part of daily operations. They ensure consistent performance and help prevent rare but potentially catastrophic incidents. This emphasis on checklists is not a reflection of professionals’ lack of competence; rather, even highly skilled experts benefit from structured cognitive aids in complex environments [ , ]. In recent years, the healthcare sector has increasingly adopted safety strategies similar to those used in aviation. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has shown significant improvements in perioperative outcomes and team coordination across various clinical settings. Regional anaesthesia shares many characteristics with aviation; it is a high-skill discipline that requires precise execution under time pressure and involves low-incidence but high-impact risks. Therefore, a structured checklist should be regarded as a practical safety tool rather than merely an administrative formality. It reinforces good clinical practices and helps clinicians provide reliable and consistent care [ , ]. Italian data further support the safety profile of regional anesthesia. The RICALOR prospective registry, involving 17 Italian hospitals and over 117,000 procedures, reported that regional anesthesia represented 54.3% of anesthetic techniques. The overall complication rate was 4.6 per 10,000 procedures, while major complications were extremely rare (0.07/1000). These findings confirm that regional anesthesia is widely practiced in Italy with a high safety profile, but also underline the importance of continuous monitoring and structured reporting systems to maintain and improve patient safety [ ]. Among the potential complications of regional anaesthesia, neurological injury is one of the most serious and concerning adverse events. The pathophysiology of neurological injury is multifactorial, involving aspects such as mechanical trauma, ischemic or inflammatory mechanisms, local anaesthetic neurotoxicity, or a combination of these factors. The risk of these injuries can be exacerbated by inadequate monitoring or suboptimal techniques. A crucial safety aspect that warrants attention is the prevention of Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST), a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of regional anesthesia. A structured checklist may also contribute to reducing the risk and LAST and neurotoxicity. While a checklist cannot eliminate pharmacological risk, it can promote adherence to key safety behaviors such as dose verification, awareness of cumulative dosing, incremental injection with aspiration, appropriate monitoring, and readiness for emergency management. In addition, checklist-driven workflows may facilitate early recognition of prodromal LAST symptoms and prompt treatment, which are crucial determinants of patient outcomes [ , ]. Despite advancements in ultrasound guidance and dose-limiting strategies, LAST continues to be reported in various clinical settings, often resulting from inaccurate dosing, inadvertent intravascular injection, or delayed recognition of early warning symptoms [ ]. To enhance clinician vigilance throughout all procedural phases, it is beneficial to incorporate structured checklist elements specifically designed to prevent LAST. Key preventive measures should include systematic dose calculations based on patient factors, aspiration before injection, incremental dosing with frequent verbal communication about cumulative volume, and real-time monitoring to detect neurological or cardiovascular warning signs [ ]. Furthermore, integrating explicit reminders to confirm the immediate availability of lipid emulsion therapy and the presence of a skilled response team reinforces institutional readiness for emergency management. Checklists serve not only as cognitive aids but also as educational tools that promote a culture of safety, consolidating good practices and ensuring team alignment around shared safety standards. Therefore, their role extends beyond mere documentation, becoming an integral component of harm-reduction strategies designed to minimize the incidence and severity of LAST [ ]. The theoretical model proposed in this study offers a practical and organized approach to quantifying the potential organizational, safety, and economic benefits of implementing the LRA checklist in clinical practice, as suggested by Mulroy et al. [ ]. One of its key strengths is its simplicity and replicability. The model relies on a limited number of easily obtainable institutional variables, including annual procedural volume, staff cost per minute, estimated time savings, baseline complication rate, expected relative risk reduction, and cost of complications. This allows hospitals with different organizational structures to adapt to their local context without requiring complex statistical expertise. Additionally, the model provides a transparent framework that links the use of checklists to measurable outcomes. This transparency facilitates communication with hospital management and supports informed decision-making regarding resource allocation and patient safety investments. Importantly, the checklist underwent a structured content validation through a modified Delphi process involving 15 experts from the ESRA Italian chapter Board, which enhances its methodological rigor and supports the content validity of the tool. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the model is based on theoretical assumptions and preliminary estimates derived from literature-based ranges and expert opinions; therefore, real-world data may vary across institutions. The projected reductions in complications and time savings, while consistent with published evidence on perioperative safety tools, may either underestimate or overestimate the true impact depending on baseline compliance with safety standards and staff engagement. Second, quantifying the economic value of medico-legal benefits is challenging due to variability in institutional risk management policies and national legal frameworks. Third, the model primarily focuses on direct and short-term outcomes, while long-term effects, such as cultural change, improved team performance, enhanced training quality, and patient-reported outcomes, are not addressed [ ]. Finally, external validation in diverse clinical settings, ideally through multicenter prospective studies, will be essential to assess generalizability, confirm cost-effectiveness, and refine model parameters. 4.1. Perspectives: Implementation Strategy Successful integration of the LRA checklist into routine clinical practice requires a structured implementation strategy that focuses on training, workflow alignment, and sustained staff engagement. Before deployment, it is essential to conduct targeted education sessions for anesthesiologists, residents, and nursing staff to ensure they understand the checklist’s structure, objectives, and medico-legal significance. Introducing the checklist through short simulation-based workshops or real-time demonstrations can enhance usability and encourage adherence. Local champions or “checklist facilitators” can support the initial implementation by providing on-site guidance and feedback, especially during the early adoption phase. To minimize workflow disruption and promote consistent use, the checklist should be clearly integrated into existing perioperative pathways, either in paper form or embedded into electronic medical records.

One priority area is the broader implementation of objective injection pressure monitoring devices such as the BSmart™ Injection Pressure Monitor (B. Braun Medical, Melsungen, Germany) and the SAFIRA ® —SAFer Injection for Regional Anaesthesia system (Medovate Ltd., Cambridge, UK) [ , , ]. The BSmart™ device provides inline, colour-coded feedback on injection pressure during peripheral nerve blocks, offering an objective and quantifiable alternative to subjective “syringe feel” and facilitating documentation of injection pressures within predefined ranges. Similarly, the SAFIRA ® system integrates a safety mechanism that automatically limits the maximum injection pressure and allows the clinician to control both aspiration and infusion with a single operator workflow, potentially reducing the risk of injection at pressures associated with neural injury. Regular audits and feedback cycles, along with periodic reviews of checklist items and outcome data, will help monitor compliance and identify areas for improvement. Finally, involving frontline clinicians in ongoing updates will strengthen ownership, reduce resistance, and foster a sustainable safety culture within regional anesthesia practice. An additional important determinant of real-world effectiveness is checklist adherence. The potential clinical and organizational benefits described in the theoretical model assume appropriate and consistent implementation. Variability in compliance rates across institutions may significantly influence outcomes, as demonstrated in other checklist based safety interventions. Future prospective studies should therefore assess not only complication trends but also checklist utilization rates and quality of completion, in order to better understand the relationship between adherence and safety impact. 4.2. Strengths and Limitations The questionnaire consisted of structured multiple-choice items using Likert-scale response options (ranging from strong disagreement to strong agreement). Questions addressed perceived necessity of a regional anesthesia checklist, expected impact on patient safety, educational value, and potential medico-legal benefits. The survey was exploratory and descriptive in nature and was not designed as a validated psychometric instrument. (We added survey results in ) This study adds to the expanding field of safety standardization in regional anesthesia by introducing a carefully developed checklist and a new method for evaluating its impact in healthcare institutions. One of the study’s key strengths is its dual focus: the LRA checklist was created and validated through expert consensus, while also being situated within a broader framework that considers workflow efficiency, legal protection, and organizational value. By incorporating a theoretical model, the study provides a fresh perspective for decision-makers, which could enhance administrative acceptance, an aspect that is often overlooked in literature on checklists. Model parameters were based on conservative, literature-informed assumptions and institutional plausibility ranges rather than empirical prospective data. The estimated absolute reduction in complication probability (ΔPerror) was modeled using cautious ranges extrapolated from published evidence on checklist-based safety interventions in perioperative settings. The documentation-related benefit (Cdoc) was conceptualized as a proxy for improved medico-legal traceability and risk mitigation, acknowledging that such benefits are difficult to quantify directly. These parameters were intentionally conservative to avoid overestimation of economic impact. The model is therefore intended as a structured decision-support framework rather than a formal cost-effectiveness analysis. A one-way sensitivity analysis was performed to explore the robustness of the model under conservative and plausible variations in key assumptions. In addition to varying the relative reduction in complication-related costs (20–40%), we varied net time saved per procedure (1–3 min) and examined the effect of different annual procedure volumes in scaling scenarios. All other parameters were held constant. This approach allowed assessment of model stability without introducing excessive analytical complexity. However, the study does have limitations. It does not include real-world implementation data, so the projected benefits remain theoretical. The model also fails to account for cultural, behavioral, or organizational factors that can significantly influence the adoption of safety tools. Furthermore, the checklist was specifically tailored to the Italian healthcare setting, which may limit its generalizability until it is adapted and tested in other healthcare systems. Its creation followed a rigorous methodology, which included expert validation of the content. Additionally, a theoretical model suggested potential organizational and economic benefits for healthcare institutions. While these findings are preliminary, they support the integration of the LRA checklist into routine clinical practice as part of a larger patient safety strategy. The effectiveness of checklist implementation should be evaluated through prospective audits measuring adherence to checklist items, quality of documentation, and trends in complication recognition. chunks.content: Introduction Spinal anesthesia is still the recommended method of anesthesia for elective cesarean delivery [ ]. The resulting sympathetic block precipitates high incidence of maternal hypotension with unfavorable maternal and fetal outcomes. These include maternal nausea and vomiting, hemodynamic instability, and disturbed conscious level [ ]. The decreased uteroplacental perfusion have potential deleterious consequences for the fetus [ ]. The pathophysiology of spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension in obstetric patients primarily involves sympathetic blockade leading to vasodilation, with decreased systemic vascular resistance being the predominant mechanism rather than reduced venous return [ ]. While vasopressors effectively normalize blood pressure, maintaining adequate maternal cardiac output (CO) represents a distinct and crucial goal during cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. Phenylephrine, despite its efficacy in restoring blood pressure, can significantly reduce maternal CO by up to 20% through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction and reflex bradycardia [ , ], highlighting the limitation of using blood pressure as the sole indicator of maternal hemodynamic adequacy. Various protocols for intravascular volume management during neuraxial anesthesia for cesarean delivery exhibit considerable heterogeneity regarding fluid composition (crystalloid versus colloid), administration timing (prophylactic preload versus synchronous coload), and volumetric dosing parameters [ ]. Evidence consistently demonstrates that crystalloid preload exhibits negligible prophylactic efficacy against spinal-induced hypotension, whereas alternative regimens, including colloid preload and either crystalloid or colloid coload protocols, demonstrate comparable hemodynamic stabilization properties based on current literature [ ]. Efforts to optimize intravascular volume through colloid administration have produced inconsistent effects on maternal CO, with some studies demonstrating significant improvements [ ] while others report minimal impact [ , ]. However, colloids offer theoretical advantages through sustained intravascular volume expansion due to higher oncotic pressure and prolonged plasma retention [ , ]. Human albumin, in particular, provides physiologically compatible oncotic support with superior safety compared to synthetic colloids, which face increasing regulatory restrictions [ ]. Despite these theoretical benefits, the specific cardiac effects of combining albumin preload with crystalloid coload, as measured by modern hemodynamic monitoring, remain unexplored. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) has emerged as a valuable tool for real-time hemodynamic assessment in anesthesia and critical care, offering direct visualization of cardiac function and volume status [ , ]. Unlike indirect measures such as blood pressure, TTE provides direct assessment of stroke volume (SV), CO, and preload indices including velocity time integral (VTI). However, its systematic application in obstetric anesthesia remains limited, particularly for evaluating fluid strategies during cesarean delivery [ ]. We specifically compared albumin preload combined with crystalloid coload versus standard crystalloid coload alone because: (1) crystalloid coload represents current standard care, (2) this combination allows pragmatic implementation without abandoning established protocols, and (3) modest albumin volumes may provide hemodynamic benefits while minimizing cost. We hypothesized that 250 mL albumin 5% preload combined with 750 mL crystalloid coload would better maintain maternal cardiac output temporal patterns compared to 1000 mL crystalloid coload alone, as measured serially by TTE during cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. Patient and methods This prospective randomized controlled, double-blind trial complied with Declaration of Helsinki principles and followed Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines. Prior to subject enrollment, the protocol was reviewed and approved by the Regional Research Ethics Committee, registered at the National Committee of BIO&MED. Ethics (NCBE) NO. H-04-Q-001, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Ministry of health, Al-Qassim Region, and was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT06654687 ; principal investigator: Mohamed A. Tolba; date of registration: (October 22, 2024). The study was conducted at the obstetrics and gynecology operation room, at Qassim University Medical City, from 27/10/2024 to 25/3/2025. The 1 st case was enrolled on 27/10/2024. Eligible participants were American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status II parturients with full-term singleton pregnancy who were scheduled for elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. The exclusion criteria comprised height < 150 cm, weight < 55 kg, and body mass index ≥ 40 kg/m2; women in labor or with contraindications to spinal anesthesia (patient refusal, elevated intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, or local skin infection); chronic or gestational hypertension; baseline systolic blood pressure > 140 mmHg; hemoglobin < 10 g/dL; diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or renal diseases; and polyhydramnios or fetal anomalies. Written informed consent was taken from eligible participants on the day of the procedure. The study participants were randomized via R statistical software version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Participants were randomly allocated to two equal groups (combination and crystalloid) utilizing the permuted block randomization technique with randomly chosen block sizes of 4 and 6. Group allocation was concealed using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes prepared by a statistician not involved in patient care or outcome assessment. Another investigator (N.S.A), blinded (to types of fluids), titrated the phenylephrine dose, and administered ephedrine and glycopyrrolate when required. These two investigators in addition to the fluid bags and the infusion syringe containing phenylephrine were separated by an opaque sheet from the patients and the other investigators who assessed the intraoperative outcomes. The first investigator (M.A.T.) and another three investigators (R.A.A), (A.F.A), and (R.S.A) recorded the baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) and heart rate (HR), and (M.A.T.) obtained the baseline TTE images, then left the operating room and returned immediately after administration of spinal anesthesia to record the intraoperative and outcome data (systolic BP, heart rate, TTE images, APGAR score at 1 and 5 min, ephedrine and glycopyrrolate requirements, total phenylephrine dose, incidence of nausea/vomiting, and the urine output). Study protocol Baseline measurements Study participants were positioned supine with a 15° left lateral tilt on the operating table using an obstetric wedge. Standard monitors were attached to all patients (noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximeter, and electrocardiography). Baseline hemodynamic parameters (SBP and HR) were recorded following a stabilization period, utilizing mean values from three consecutive measurements at 2-minute intervals. Basal TTE images were obtained typically before administration of any type of fluids and before conduction of spinal anesthesia. Fluid interventions All patients received two 18-gauge IV lines in the right forearm. The combination group received 250 mL of human albumin 5% (BAXTER, Austria) via infusion pump over 10 min before spinal anesthesia, followed by 750 mL Ringer’s lactate over 5 min coinciding with intrathecal injection. The crystalloid group received 1000 mL Ringer’s lactate over 5 min at the time of intrathecal injection. To maintain blinding, patients in the crystalloid coload group underwent a 10-minute sham procedure with non-opened IV lines attached. In both groups, Ringer’s lactate at 1 mL/min was administered as a maintenance fluid until cord clamping. Anesthesia technique Neuraxial anesthesia was performed in the sitting position utilizing a 27-gauge pencil point spinal needle at L3-L4 interspace, administering hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg with fentanyl 15 mcg intrathecally. Spinal anesthesia was conducted, and the APGAR score was assessed respectively by an anesthesiologist and a pediatrician not involved in the study. After SA administration, all patients were positioned in the left lateral position. Surgery proceeded only after confirming adequate anesthesia (minimum upper sensory level of T4 via pinprick testing); patients failing to reach this threshold were excluded from the study as inadequate anesthesia necessitating conversion to general anesthesia or supplemental neuraxial medication would fundamentally alter the hemodynamic profile under investigation. Following delivery and cord clamping, phenylephrine infusion was discontinued, and patients received 10 IU oxytocin diluted in 500 mL Ringer’s lactate solution delivered intravenously over 1 h. Hemodynamic management protocol Prophylactic phenylephrine infusion was initiated in both groups at 50 mcg/min at the time of intrathecal injection and continued until delivery. The infusion was titrated by the blinded investigator (N.S.A.) according to a standardized protocol: the rate was increased to 50–75 mcg/min if SBP decreased by > 20% from baseline, and to 75–100 mcg/min if SBP decreased by > 30% from baseline. The infusion was decreased or temporarily stopped if SBP exceeded baseline values. For hypotension accompanied by bradycardia (HR < 60 bpm), ephedrine 5 mg IV bolus was administered instead of increasing phenylephrine. If bradycardia persisted despite ephedrine treatment, glycopyrrolate 0.1 mg IV was given. This protocol was uniformly applied to all patients in both groups. Outcome measurements and timepoints Cardiovascular parameters (SBP and HR) were monitored at 1-minute intervals until delivery, then every 3 min until surgery completion. Hypotension (defined as SBP decrease > 20% from baseline) and bradycardia (HR < 60 beats per minute) were treated by the previously mentioned standardized hemodynamic management. CO, SV and VTI were measured at five key timepoints: baseline, 1 and 5 min after spinal anesthesia, immediately after delivery, and 1 h post-delivery. VTI measurements were obtained by averaging 3–5 consecutive cardiac cycles to minimize beat-to-beat variability. The CSA measurement derived from LVOT diameter was obtained once at baseline as this represents a stable anatomical parameter that does not change acutely with hemodynamic variations. SV was calculated using the 2 variables CSA and VTI across the LVOT according to the following equation, SV = CSA (cm2) × VTI (cm), CO was serially measured noninvasively using the following equation, CO = SV × HR. The primary outcome was the changes in CO at subsequent time points compared between groups. Secondary outcomes included: the SV changes compared between groups at subsequent time points, VTI changes compared between groups at subsequent time points, total phenylephrine dose, total ephedrine dose, total glycopyrrolate dose, incidence of hypotension, incidence of bradycardia, incidence of nausea and/or vomiting, APGAR score at l and 5 min, urine output at 1 h after end of the study. Sample size calculation The sample size was estimated for the primary outcome (CO) using a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) framework. Based on pilot data, the baseline CO standard deviation was 1.44 L/min with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.42 across repeated measurements. Five spaced time points were planned. The minimal clinically important difference for the group-by-time interaction was set at 0.64 L/min (≈ 10% change from baseline), representing the smallest physiologically relevant improvement likely to enhance uteroplacental perfusion. A random intercept for subject and normally distributed residuals were assumed. Power was assessed by simulation (500 iterations per scenario) in (R Core Team, 2024; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the lme4 package. For each simulated dataset, we compared the full model including the group-by-time interaction with a nested model excluding the interaction, using a likelihood ratio test at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Statistical analysis Statistical analyses and data visualization were conducted using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All 162 randomized patients achieved adequate anesthesia and completed the study; therefore, no patients were excluded from analysis. There were no missing data for primary or secondary outcomes; all participants completed all planned measurements. Distribution normality was assessed via histogram analysis and Kolmogorov-Smirnov testing. Data presentation followed standard statistical formats: mean ± standard deviation for normal distributions, median (range) for non-normal distributions, and number (percentage) for categorical variables. Intergroup comparisons utilized Mann-Whitney U test for non-parametric outcomes and chi-square analysis for categorical variables. The SV changes, total phenylephrine dose, total ephedrine dose, total glycopyrrolate dose, incidence of hypotension, incidence of bradycardia, incidence of nausea and/or vomiting, and APGAR score at l and 5 min did not significantly differ between the two groups. VTI measurements at different time points and urine output at 1 h after the end of the study were higher significantly in the combination group. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use TTE to directly compare the effects of human albumin preload combined with crystalloid coload versus crystalloid coload alone on cardiac function during cesarean delivery. We selected temporal CO dynamics as our primary outcome rather than static point measurements because this longitudinal approach comprehensively evaluates each fluid strategy’s capacity to maintain cardiovascular stability throughout critical perioperative transitions, including neuraxial blockade, surgical intervention, and post-delivery recalibration. This addresses the clinically relevant question: ‘Which strategy better preserves CO throughout the entire procedure?’ rather than at isolated moments, avoiding the risk of missing important hemodynamic response and recovery patterns. We used 250 mL of 5% albumin to balance efficacy with cost-effectiveness. Albumin provides physiologically compatible oncotic pressure with superior safety compared to synthetic colloids, avoiding coagulopathy, tissue accumulation, and potential renal dysfunction [ ]. This modest volume was selected based on pilot data from our institution demonstrating adequate hemodynamic effects, and pharmacokinetic principles demonstrating sustained plasma expansion despite limited volume [ ]. Our intent was to test whether a small, pragmatic albumin preload alters cardiac filling dynamics. Recent regulatory restrictions on synthetic colloids [ ] make this albumin-based approach particularly relevant for contemporary obstetric practice. CO measurements showed similar trends between groups without statistically significant differences, though the combination group trended toward higher values at 1-minute post-spinal (difference 329.4 mL, p = 0.0663) and post-delivery (difference 327.6 mL, p = 0.0678). Both groups reached maximum CO post-delivery (approximately 7.5 L) before returning to near-baseline at 1-hour, aligning with physiological timelines documented in both historical [ ] and contemporary studies [ ] showing CO normalization within 60–90 min post-delivery These findings parallel McDonald et al. [ ] who reported modestly higher CO with colloid (0.5–0.7 L/min difference) that also did not reach significance, suggesting both fluid strategies adequately maintained CO during critical perioperative periods. However, VTI measurements revealed significant differences between groups, with the combination group demonstrating higher values at both 1-minute post-spinal anesthesia (difference of 1.87 cm, p = 0.0024) and at 1-hour post-study (difference of 1.40 cm, p = 0.0233). VTI measures the distance that blood travels during each ejection phase. Unlike CO, VTI provides a more direct reflection of cardiac filling and preload conditions without being confounded by the compensatory mechanisms, [ , ] offering a more reliable indicator of volume status and potentially explaining the significant VTI differences observed in our study despite similar CO measurements. As colloids have higher oncotic pressure and remain in the intravascular space longer, [ ] this leads to more sustained plasma volume expansion and more effective prevention of hypotension than crystalloid pre-load [ ]. These points could explain both, the 1-minute post-spinal difference (1.87 cm) indicating better initial volume status and maintained cardiac filling due to the effect of the administration of

cardiac filling and preload conditions without being confounded by the compensatory mechanisms, [ , ] offering a more reliable indicator of volume status and potentially explaining the significant VTI differences observed in our study despite similar CO measurements. As colloids have higher oncotic pressure and remain in the intravascular space longer, [ ] this leads to more sustained plasma volume expansion and more effective prevention of hypotension than crystalloid pre-load [ ]. These points could explain both, the 1-minute post-spinal difference (1.87 cm) indicating better initial volume status and maintained cardiac filling due to the effect of the administration of 250-mL colloid before spinal anesthesia, and the persistent difference at 1-hour (1.40 cm) demonstrating sustained effect of colloids. The observed VTI increase of 1.32 cm corresponds to approximately 5 mL additional stroke volume per beat, equating to 0.3–0.5 L/min increased CO (4–8% over baseline) at typical heart rates. However, the clinical significance remains speculative. Despite statistical significance, this VTI advantage did not translate into reduced vasopressor requirements ( p = 0.142), improved neonatal outcomes ( p > 0.78), or fewer maternal adverse events. Whether this difference would benefit higher-risk populations (cardiac disease, preeclampsia, hemorrhage) requires adequately powered, outcome-focused trials. These findings are hypothesis-generating, not definitive evidence of clinical superiority. Temporal hemodynamic analysis showed significant intergroup differences in both pre- and post-delivery phases. Pre-delivery, the combination group had lower heart rates at minutes 1, 2, and 5 ( p < 0.05), indicating reduced chronotropic response. Similarly, SBP measurements showed greater stability in the combination group, with significant differences at minutes 2 and 4 ( p < 0.05). This hemodynamic advantage persisted into the post-delivery phase, where the combination group maintained more consistent SBP parameters (within a narrow range 114–115 mmHg) and exhibited less HR variability at multiple timepoints (minutes 9, 18, and 21; p < 0.05). These findings partially parallel our previous investigation [ ] comparing synthetic colloid preload with crystalloid coload, which demonstrated improved SBP at 3 min post-injection, though without significant heart rate differences. Vasopressor requirements were comparable between groups, with median phenylephrine doses of 600 mcg in the combination group versus 666 mcg in the crystalloid group ( p = 0.142). Our doses align with recent studies employing prophylactic infusion protocols ranging from 500 to 1000 mcg during cesarean deliveries [ , ]. The similarity in vasopressor requirements despite different fluid strategies suggests that prophylactic phenylephrine effectively maintained maternal blood pressure regardless of fluid choice. Maternal and neonatal outcomes were excellent in both groups. APGAR scores at 1 and 5 min were comparable (median 9 and 10, respectively; p > 0.78), indicating adequate uteroplacental perfusion. The combination group had significantly higher urine output (350 vs. 300 mL, p = 0.038), possibly reflecting different fluid distribution patterns. Nausea and vomiting incidence were similar between groups (21% vs. 30.9%, p = 0.148). Some issues should be acknowledged. First, while we observed trends in CO differences, the study may have been underpowered to detect statistically significant differences in this primary outcome. Second, despite using standardized TTE techniques following American Society of Echocardiography guidelines, these measurements can be technically challenging in the perioperative setting, particularly post-delivery due to movement artifacts during surgery and interference from surgical instruments and cautery. We tried to address this by minimizing the probe manipulation time and efficient communication with the surgical team. Also, while our TTE measurements were performed by a single experienced operator, we did not formally assess intra-rater variability or reproducibility. Future studies should include formal reproducibility assessments with blinded re-analysis of stored images to quantify measurement precision. Third, we limited the analysis of the predelivery serial changes in HR and SBP up to 5 min after intrathecal injection, which was the shortest spinal-to-delivery time, potentially missing later effects. Fourth, given the significant impact of nausea and vomiting and fetal outcomes on these types of patients, we recommend that future research specifically investigate the direct effects of fluid management strategies on these patient-centered outcomes to optimize patient care. Finally, our protocol focused specifically on SBP as this is the most used parameter for defining and managing spinal-induced hypotension in cesarean delivery and aligns with most published studies in this field. However, diastolic and mean arterial pressure measurements would have provided additional hemodynamic information, particularly regarding perfusion pressure, and should be considered in future investigations. In conclusion, this randomized controlled trial found no statistically significant difference in the temporal patterns of CO (group-by-time interaction) between combination albumin preload plus crystalloid coload versus crystalloid coload alone during cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. While the combination strategy showed improvements in VTI measurements and urine output, these differences did not translate into clinically meaningful improvements in vasopressor requirements, maternal hemodynamic stability, or neonatal outcomes. chunks.content: Introduction Cadaveric dissection remains the gold standard for understanding three-dimensional relationships of nerves, muscles, fascial planes, and vascular structures. Handling real tissue provides tactile feedback on fascial compliance and needle-tissue interaction that no simulation can fully replicate. In the practice of regional anesthesia, where precise needle placement determines block success, cadavers serve as “silent teachers” to bridge textbook anatomy and live-patient variability.[ ] There are various embalming techniques, each with its advantages and disadvantages. The techniques are Thiel soft embalming, formalin-based embalming, fresh-frozen cadavers, saturated salt solution, and plastination.[ ] Thiel or soft-embalmed cadavers offer realistic ultrasound image quality, enabling trainees to master sonoanatomy before live-patient practice. The various peripheral nerve blocks and fascial plane blocks have been validated and implemented into practice only after understanding the spread dynamics done in cadavers. These studies help in understanding the extent of spread, the direction of the spread, and the possible dermatomal coverage. Bibliometric analysis, a form of quantitative research that examines networks, patterns, and trends within a particular field of study, is used to assess various aspects of published academic literature. To assess research productivity, citation dynamics, and collaborations between researchers, institutions, and nations, this approach makes use of tools and validated software. Bibliometric studies identify influential works, point out research gaps, and offer insightful information about how knowledge has evolved—all of which help to direct future research.[ ] To date, no bibliometric analysis has been done on cadaveric studies related to regional anesthesia. This article aims for a bibliometric analysis to know the various research trends, prolific authors, institutes, countries, journals, and the citation metrics of publications related to cadaveric studies pertaining to regional anesthesia. Methods We searched the literature from its inception to May 2025. We conducted a comprehensive search on the Scopus database using the following search strategy: (TITLE-ABS-KEY (cadaveric AND study) OR TITLE-ABS-KEY (cadaveric AND dissection) OR TITLE-ABS-KEY (cadaveric AND experiments) AND TITLE-ABS-KEY (regional AND anesthesia) OR TITLE-ABS-KEY (nerve AND block)) AND (EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “VETE”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “AGRI”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “ENGI”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “MATE”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “COMP”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “SOCI”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “MATH”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “ENVI”) OR EXCLUDE (SUBJAREA, “EART”)) The Scopus file was stored in comma-separated values (CSV) format. The CSV file was systematically screened by two authors (PMN and RN). Articles in which there were no details about cadaveric studies related to regional anesthesia, peripheral nerve block, or fascial plane block were removed. The final articles were processed for bibliometric analysis. Data processing After removing the ineligible articles and cited references, the included hits were exported for analysis. For bibliometric analysis, VOSviewer (Version 1.6.20, Leiden University, the Netherlands) was used.[ ] We planned five different kinds of analysis using the VOS viewer. These analyses included bibliographic coupling, citation, co-authorship, co-occurrence, and co-citation. The units of analysis for co-authorship analysis were countries, organizations, and authors. The units of analysis for co-occurrence were index, author, and all keywords. Discussion This bibliometric analysis has utilized several quantitative tools, like publication counts, citation networks, and co-word clustering, to identify research trends and the influence of authors, organizations, and various sources publishing the various categories of these documents. Cadaveric studies in regional anesthesia provide a controlled environment to visualize injectate spread, improve sonoanatomy, and test mechanistic hypotheses that would be unethical or impossible to perform prospectively in patients. Cadaveric dye-dissection studies provide the three-dimensional roadmap necessary to refine block techniques, understand the flow dynamics, and prevent complications.[ ] Quantitative imaging in embalmed specimens uncovers variability that can inform clinical volume and needle-placement guidelines. High-fidelity cadaver simulators bridge the gap between synthetic phantoms and live-patient scenarios, enhancing trainee confidence and safety. The results of the various cadaveric studies can be useful for practical refinements across technique, safety, training, and quality assurance in regional anesthesia. These articles help in refining the block technique, improving the needle trajectory, facilitating competency, and increasing confidence in performing various blocks, better safety profile of the blocks due to better understanding, all leading to better analgesic efficacy and successful blocks. McLeod et al. [ ] assessed the characteristics of the US-guided axillary approach to brachial plexus block in two Thiel embalmed cadavers. The authors mentioned that it was easy to identify the nerves, track the needles, perceive the fluid surrounding the nerves after injection, and detect intraneural injections by accident. Studies showed how the injectate spread and also helped in understanding the mechanism of action of these blocks.[ ] While cadaveric dissection offers unrivaled three-dimensional anatomical fidelity, a multimodal approach to anesthesia training enhances skill acquisition, retention, and patient safety. Key complementary methods include ultrasound phantoms and gel models, high-fidelity manikins and simulators, animal tissue models, virtual and augmented reality platforms, and 3D-printed models. This bibliometric analysis has several limitations. We searched only the Scopus database. The Web of Science, PubMed, Lens, and Dimensions databases are additional resources that can be utilized for bibliometric analysis. The software does, however, allow analysis of the output produced by a single database. As a result, the analysis could have overlooked some articles. Because new articles were continually added to the literature after this analysis was submitted for review, those published after the date of our data collection were not included. We did not analyze the studies based on the type of cadavers used (Thiel, fresh) or the type of dye used (methylene blue, latex), or the use of radiography in studying the cadavers. Conclusions This bibliometric analysis analyzes the research trends, most cited authors and articles, and also the relationship between authors and their cited work. It appears that the literature remains concentrated in a few high-income academic centers, with limited representation from resource-limited settings. Enhanced collaboration between anatomists, anaesthesiologists, and imaging specialists will be essential to translate cadaveric findings into safer, more effective regional anesthesia protocols. chunks.content: ASRA Pain Medicine consensus guidelines on the management of the perioperative patient on cannabis and cannabinoids. The past two decades have seen an increase in cannabis use due to both regulatory changes and an interest in potential therapeutic effects of the substance, yet many aspects of the substance and their health implications remain controversial or unclear. In November 2020, the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine charged the Cannabis Working Group to develop guidelines for the perioperative use of cannabis. The Perioperative Use of Cannabis and Cannabinoids Guidelines Committee was charged with drafting responses to the nine key questions using a modified Delphi method with the overall goal of producing a document focused on the safe management of surgical patients using cannabinoids. A consensus recommendation required ≥75% agreement. Nine questions were selected, with 100% consensus achieved on third-round voting. Topics addressed included perioperative screening, postponement of elective surgery, concomitant use of opioid and cannabis perioperatively, implications for parturients, adjustment in anesthetic and analgesics intraoperatively, postoperative monitoring, cannabis use disorder, and postoperative concerns. Surgical patients using cannabinoids are at potential increased risk for negative perioperative outcomes. Specific clinical recommendations for perioperative management of cannabis and cannabinoids were successfully created.
